processing: As with other Yunnan cakes of its time, sun-dried large-leaf tea is steamed and pressed into a flat round cake. Little is documented about any method specific to the name.
harvest_season: Not tied to a season in what is documented; the term describes the shape and the product name.
appearance_dry: A flat round cake; old examples are dark brown.
appearance_liquor: Amber to reddish in old cakes, as is usual for aged raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Whole and broken large leaves, darkened with age in old cakes.
taste_profile: No single flavour belongs to the name. Typical of aged raw pu-erh, old cakes lean to wood and herbal depth rather than the sharper bitterness of a young cake.

brewing.notes: Brew as any raw pu-erh cake of its age: a quick rinse, then short steeps, longer as the leaf tires.

vintage_note: The word mainly survives on old wrappers: 1950s tea such as Blue Mark Round Tea iron cake and Red Lotus Round Tea appears at auction under this name. It is otherwise an antique or a retro label rather than a current grade, and a new cake printed with it is simply a modern raw or ripe cake, sold by year.
description:
Yuancha simply means 'round tea', and it is the old name on Yunnan pu-erh cakes before Seven Sons cake became the usual term. It is a shape and a product name, not a separate kind of tea.

The method is little documented under this name. Cakes of the period were generally made as other Yunnan pressed teas were, from sun-dried large leaf steamed and pressed into a disc, which keeps well and travels well.

There is no flavour to expect from the word itself. An old round tea will taste like aged raw pu-erh of its storage, and a new one like whatever the factory put in it. Brew it as you would any cake of the same age.

For a buyer the name is most useful as a date clue when reading old wrappers. It adds nothing to a new cake; judge those by year, factory and material.
history:
The name is attached to 1950s products: auction listings show Blue Mark Round Tea iron cakes and Red Lotus Round Tea from that decade. The state-era Zhongcha brand round tea was renamed Yunnan Seven Sons cake in 1972, when the Yunnan company was reorganised.

How the name itself arose is not clearly documented, though the plain meaning of 'round' points to the shape.
